name: C++ Developer (Robotics)
description: Modern C++ for real-time robotics, embedded targets, and performance-critical motion and perception stacks.

categories.name: C++ Core
categories.description: Language fundamentals, OOP, templates, and idiomatic C++ used in production codebases.

cards.question: What is the difference between stack and heap allocation in C++?
cards.answer: Automatic variables live on the stack with deterministic lifetime tied to scope. Dynamic allocation with new or make_unique places objects on the heap until explicitly freed or managed by smart pointers. Stack allocation is fast and cache-friendly; heap is for unknown size or lifetime beyond the current scope. In robotics loops, prefer stack or preallocated pools to avoid fragmentation during control cycles.

cards.question: When should you prefer references over pointers?
cards.answer: References must bind to valid objects and cannot be null or rebound, which makes APIs clearer for required dependencies. Pointers express optional or nullable targets and support polymorphism via base pointers. Use const T& for read-only inputs and T& for in-out parameters when null is impossible. In sensor interfaces, pointers often model missing data; references model always-present configuration.

cards.question: Explain RAII and why it matters on embedded systems.
cards.answer: Resource Acquisition Is Initialization ties resource lifetime to object lifetime: constructors acquire, destructors release. Locks, file handles, and DMA buffers clean up even when exceptions or early returns occur. On embedded builds with exceptions disabled, destructors still run at scope exit for stack objects. RAII prevents leaks in long-running robot processes without manual cleanup in every error path.

cards.question: What is the rule of zero and when do you deviate from it?
cards.answer: If your class needs no custom destructor, copy, or move operations, do not declare them; the compiler-generated special members are correct. Deviate when you manage raw resources, enforce unique ownership, or need custom copying semantics. std::unique_ptr members often keep you at rule-of-zero. Robot driver wrappers around hardware handles typically need custom move-only types.

cards.question: How do move semantics improve performance?
cards.answer: Move construction and assignment transfer resources from a source object without deep copies, leaving the source in a valid empty state. They activate on rvalues and via std::move for explicit transfers. Large std::vector or point cloud buffers become cheap to return from perception pipelines. Misusing std::move on const objects silently copies instead of moving.

cards.question: What is the difference between struct and class in C++?
cards.answer: Only default member access differs: public for struct, private for class. Inheritance defaults differ similarly. Teams often use struct for plain data aggregates and class for invariants and behavior. POD-style structs map cleanly to sensor messages shared with C APIs. Consistency with project style matters more than the keyword itself.

cards.question: When are templates preferable to virtual functions?
cards.answer: Templates instantiate specialized code at compile time with zero runtime dispatch overhead. They excel for generic math, containers, and fixed-size Eigen-style operations in hot loops. Virtual functions provide runtime polymorphism with stable binary interfaces across modules. Robotics code often combines both: templates in inner loops, virtual drivers at hardware boundaries.

cards.question: What is SFINAE and how is it used in practice today?
cards.answer: Substitution Failure Is Not An Error removes invalid template overloads during overload resolution instead of hard errors. It enabled enable_if-based constraints before concepts. Modern code prefers requires clauses and concepts for clearer errors. Legacy middleware still uses SFINAE traits for serializable message types.

cards.question: How do you avoid object slicing when passing polymorphic types?
cards.answer: Passing a derived object by value into a base parameter slices off derived data and behavior. Use pointers or references to base, or std::unique_ptr<Base> for ownership. Factory functions return unique_ptr to concrete types behind abstract interfaces. Slicing bugs show up as mysteriously wrong virtual calls in robot state machines.

cards.question: What is std::optional and when use it in robot APIs?
cards.answer: std::optional<T> models a value that may be absent without sentinel magic numbers. It makes missing joint limits or calibration data explicit in the type system. Access via value_or or check has_value before dereferencing. It replaces out-parameters and bool return plus reference patterns for clearer call sites.

cards.question: How do you apply stack versus heap allocation in day-to-day C++ Core work?
cards.answer: Stack allocation ties lifetime to scope and is extremely fast for small, short-lived objects. Heap allocation via new or smart pointers supports unknown size and longer lifetimes but adds allocator cost and fragmentation risk. In robotics control loops, prefer stack or preallocated pools for per-tick temporaries.

categories.name: Memory & Performance
categories.description: Allocation strategies, cache behavior, and tuning control and perception hot paths.

cards.question: Why can frequent small heap allocations hurt a real-time control loop?
cards.answer: Allocators may lock, traverse freelists, or trigger system calls with unpredictable latency. Fragmentation increases over long runtimes on embedded Linux. Spikes break deterministic cycle times for motor commands. Preallocate buffers, use arena allocators, or lock-free pools for per-tick work.

cards.question: What is cache locality and how do you improve it?
cards.answer: CPUs fetch memory in cache lines; accessing nearby data is faster than scattered pointers. Structure-of-arrays versus array-of-structures trades depend on access patterns in kinematics kernels. Keep hot fields contiguous and avoid chasing linked lists in inner loops. Profile with perf to see LLC misses before micro-optimizing.

cards.question: When should you mark functions noexcept?
cards.answer: noexcept promises the function will not throw, enabling optimizations and safe use in destructors and move operations. std::vector reallocation uses move only when move is noexcept. On -fno-exceptions builds the marker still documents intent. Do not mark noexcept if underlying code might throw unless you catch internally.

cards.question: Compare std::vector reserve versus resize for sensor buffers.
cards.answer: reserve allocates capacity without changing size, avoiding reallocation on subsequent push_back. resize changes logical size and value-initializes new elements. For fixed-rate lidar scans, reserve once at startup to the max points per revolution. resize each frame only if you need indexed access for the full slot count.

cards.question: What is false sharing and how do you mitigate it?
cards.answer: Two threads updating different variables on the same cache line cause expensive coherence traffic. Padding atomic counters or per-thread accumulators onto separate cache lines fixes many cases. It appears when parallelizing telemetry or joint state publishers. alignas(64) is a common mitigation on x86 and ARM servers.

cards.question: How does compiler inlining affect embedded builds?
cards.answer: Inlining removes call overhead and enables further optimizations across function boundaries. Aggressive -O3 can inflate code size and I-cache pressure on MCUs. Always measure on target hardware with representative workloads. hot and cold attributes guide placement when the toolchain supports them.

cards.question: What are placement new and when are they used?
cards.answer: Placement new constructs an object at a preallocated address without allocating memory. Useful for memory pools, shared memory segments, and deterministic firmware heaps. You must manually call the destructor before reusing the storage. Misaligned or undersized buffers cause undefined behavior.

cards.question: Why prefer std::array over C arrays in modern C++?
cards.answer: std::array knows its size, supports standard algorithms, and can be copied and compared safely. It avoids decay to pointer bugs in template code. Fixed-size Jacobians and rotation matrices fit naturally as std::array or Eigen fixed types. Zero overhead compared to raw arrays when optimized.

cards.question: How do you profile CPU usage of a robotics node on Linux?
cards.answer: Use perf record and perf report for hotspot functions and call graphs. Combine with clock_gettime around critical sections for lightweight tracing when perf is unavailable. Flamegraphs highlight unexpected string formatting or logging in control paths. Always profile release builds with debug symbols separately.

cards.question: What is memory alignment and why do SIMD and DMA care?
cards.answer: Types have alignment requirements; unaligned access can trap or slow on some ARM cores. SIMD loads often need 16 or 32 byte alignment. DMA engines require buffer boundaries aligned to device rules. alignas and aligned allocators prevent subtle hardware faults in camera capture pipelines.

categories.name: Concurrency
categories.description: Threads, atomics, lock-free patterns, and real-time scheduling concerns.

cards.question: What is a data race in C++ and how do you prevent it?
cards.answer: A data race occurs when two threads access the same non-atomic object and at least one write is not synchronized. Use mutexes, atomics, or message passing so happens-before relationships exist. ThreadSanitizer catches many races in CI on x86 builds. On ARM, even word-sized torn reads motivate atomic or guarded access to shared state.

cards.question: When is std::mutex enough versus a lock-free queue?
cards.answer: Mutexes are simple and correct for moderate contention and non-hot paths like configuration updates. Lock-free SPSC queues suit high-rate sensor handoff between capture and processing threads. Lock-free code is harder to verify and may still spin under contention. Pick mutex plus careful locking order unless profiling proves the mutex is the bottleneck.

cards.question: Explain memory ordering for std::atomic.
cards.answer: Sequential consistency is the default and easiest to reason about. Relaxed is for counters where ordering with other memory is irrelevant. acquire-release pairs publish data safely between threads without full seq_cst cost. Incorrect ordering causes subtle bugs where consumers see partially updated robot state.

cards.question: What is deadlock and how do you avoid it in multi-module robots?
cards.answer: Deadlock is a cycle of threads waiting on each other's locks. Establish a global lock hierarchy and never acquire locks in reverse order across modules. std::lock can acquire multiple mutexes atomically when needed. Timeouts and try_lock are last resorts that complicate correctness proofs.

cards.question: How does std::condition_variable coordinate producer and consumer threads?
cards.answer: Wait atomically releases the mutex and sleeps until notify; spurious wakeups require predicates in loops. Producers notify after updating shared queues under the same mutex. Used for thread pools processing perception jobs. Always pair with std::unique_lock for wait compatibility.

cards.question: What is thread affinity and when set it on a robot PC?
cards.answer: Pinning threads to cores reduces migration and improves cache warmth for real-time loops. Isolate control cores from OS housekeeping via cset or tuned irqbalance policies. NUMA-aware placement matters on dual-socket perception servers. Wrong affinity can increase jitter more than raw CPU usage suggests.

cards.question: Compare std::thread versus thread pools for navigation stacks.
cards.answer: Spawning std::thread per task adds overhead and unbounded thread counts hurt scheduling. Pools reuse workers for costmaps, planners, and IO callbacks. Set pool sizes from CPU budget and latency goals. Join or detach policies must be explicit to avoid termination races on shutdown.

cards.question: How do CAN and EtherCAT differ for actuator networks?
